name: component
intent: Give an object its behaviour by plugging independent component objects into it - one per domain of functionality - instead of growing a class hierarchy, so every domain stays decoupled and capabilities can be combined, swapped or removed at runtime.
problem: One class accumulates every behaviour its objects need (input, physics, rendering, audio, AI): reuse is only possible through inheritance, so each new combination of capabilities needs a new subclass, capabilities that only some objects need sit on every sibling that inherits them, and any method touching two domains welds those domains together for every reader. The recurring decision is where an object's behaviour should live when the set of behaviours is combinatorial rather than hierarchical.
context: Applies wherever one kind of object must be assembled from several largely independent domains of behaviour and the combinations change more often than the domains do: game entities and simulations are the classic case, but the same force appears in plugin hosts, device models and workflow steps. It pays off when domains are developed, tested or scheduled independently (separate teams, separate update rates, separate threads) and when the set of capabilities is open at runtime or defined by data (power-ups, plugins, prefabs).
benefits: Code grows linearly while capability combinations explode: one class per capability plus a generic container replaces one subclass per combination, so adding 'can fly' means adding a component instead of editing every affected type.
Each domain is isolated in its own object that knows nothing about the others, so teams own code without coordinating and a physics change cannot break rendering.

Behaviour becomes data: an entity is a description (which components are attached), so entity kinds can be configured by designers, loaded from prefabs and compared, instead of being frozen into a class body.
Capabilities can be added, removed or replaced at runtime, so an object changes what it is without changing what class it is (player input swapped for AI control, a 30-second buff, a mount).
Reuse is precise: a component written once serves every entity that needs exactly that capability - no copy-paste, no multiple-inheritance diamond, no unused inherited members.
Domains can be dispatched independently - per entity, per component type, or on separate threads - which a single class method cannot express.
Small components are easy to test in isolation: the container forwards requests and the individual domain objects are ordinary unit-testable collaborators.
tradeoffs: The object's behaviour is no longer readable in one place: to know what an entity does you must know which components it carries and in what order they run, so a debugger step-through no longer explains the program.

Components must communicate, and every option costs: shared state on the container is simple but makes communication implicit and order-dependent, direct sibling references recouple the components, and messages routed through the container require it to broadcast (a Mediator) with the added indirection.

Required components are not statically guaranteed: a lookup fails at runtime (null, or no matching entity) when the assembler forgot to attach a component, so a compiler-catchable mistake becomes a test-time or production-time bug.
Update order becomes registration or data order rather than visible call order, so ordering dependencies creep in silently and strict ordering forces an explicit system/dispatch layer.

The entity loses its own identity: pushed to the extreme it is an id plus component collections, so whole-object invariants must be enforced by queries, bundles or a coordinating system rather than by the object itself.

Every component slot is another allocation and one more indirection (pointer chase, virtual dispatch, or a query per lookup), so the pattern costs memory and cache locality unless storage is designed deliberately.

The container tends to become the new god object: 'pan-domain' state that every component reads and writes is exactly the shared mutable state the pattern was supposed to remove, and it hardens into an implicit interface between all components.
For a small, stable object model the machinery is pure overhead: a handful of concrete classes with plain fields is shorter, faster and far easier to debug than an assembler plus a dispatch loop.

participants.responsibility: Declares one narrow capability of an entity (an update/render/handle-event hook plus at most the state that capability owns) and knows nothing about the container or about sibling components.
Implements one domain - player input vs AI input, physics, graphics, audio, health - in a class that is reusable across every entity kind needing that capability.
Holds the attached components and the state shared across domains (identity, position, health) and forwards requests to the components; it defines no domain behaviour of its own.
Optional per-type dispatcher that owns all components of one class and runs them as a group, giving deterministic cross-entity update order without walking entity by entity.
Decides which components each entity kind receives and instantiates them, so an entity's composition is declared once instead of being scattered over call sites.
Stores entities and their components per type and answers queries for 'every entity having these components', replacing the container's own slot list.

use_cases: Game entities: a player, an NPC and a projectile differ only in which input/physics/graphics components they carry, and one graphics component serves all three.
Editor- or data-driven entity assembly: designers attach components in an editor or a prefab/config file and a single container class instantiates every entity kind.
Runtime capability changes: temporary invulnerability, a buff, a vehicle mount or a 'possessed by AI' state is an added or swapped component, not a new subclass.
Plugin and extension hosts where a host object exposes stable slots and third parties contribute behaviour objects attached to existing instances.
Simulation models where sensing, dynamics, planning and logging must run at different rates or on different threads while sharing one entity identity.
Large entity populations where the data-oriented realization keeps each component type contiguous in memory for cache efficiency.
Non-game applications: 2D CAD tools, robotics control systems, data-processing workflows, and interactive simulations where the same composition pattern replaces deep class hierarchies.
UI frameworks and document models: a widget or document node assembles layout, styling, event-handling and data-binding components, enabling runtime theme or behaviour swapping.
Multi-tenant SaaS or platform products where feature flags or plan tiers map directly to attached capability components on a user or workspace entity.

Workflow and pipeline orchestration: each step in a processing pipeline (fetch, validate, transform, render, export) is an independent system, and the pipeline is an entity whose component list describes the active stages.

Bevy game engine: entities are bare IDs and components are plain Rust structs in a World, and systems are ordinary functions whose parameters declare their data access so the scheduler runs them in parallel - the component model is the engine's core, not an add-on.

Unity DOTS (Entities package com.unity.entities): the same engine that ships classic GameObject components offers this pattern's data-oriented realization for large entity populations, with archetype-based storage and system-driven scheduling.

EnTT (C++ header-only ECS) ships in products beyond games - Mojang's Minecraft and Esri ArcGIS SDKs use it - showing component composition carrying capability matrices in commercial non-game software.
avoid_when: The object model is small and stable: three concrete classes with plain fields communicate intent better than a container, an assembler and a dispatch loop.
Inheritance genuinely models the domain and the is-a relation is stable and Liskov-safe; do not replace a correct two-level hierarchy with runtime composition for fashion.
Behaviour is not combinatorial: when every object of a kind permanently needs the same fixed collaborators, named fields plus dependency injection are simpler than a dynamic component list.
You need compile-time guarantees that a required capability is present - the pattern trades exactly that guarantee away; prefer explicit classes, validated bundles, or typestate.

The host framework already provides capability composition (React/SwiftUI/Compose-style component models, UI widget trees); re-implementing a container inside them just adds a second composition model.
Entity counts are tiny and the pattern would be adopted only 'to be able to switch things later': speculative pluggability is cheaper to add when the second capability actually appears.
anti_patterns: God container: pan-domain state keeps accumulating in the entity until every component reads and writes it - the coupling the pattern was meant to remove, now justified as 'shared state'.
Back-pointer soup: components hold references to every sibling they might need, so the domains end up as coupled as they were in the monolithic class.
Anemic components plus one manager: components become data-only structs while all behaviour lands in a single update manager, which then becomes the god object and the implicit owner of update order.

Inheritance rebuilt by hand: a fixed set of 'optional' components tested with type checks (instanceof/getComponent/filter) wherever behaviour is needed, so every code path still enumerates the type lattice.

ECS for its own sake: adopting data-oriented storage, queries and archetypes for a small object model with no entity-count or cache pressure, paying structural-change rules and query machinery for nothing.

Several writers, one field: two components update the same shared state (position written by physics and by animation) with no declared owner, producing order-dependent bugs that only appear under some dispatches.
Archetype fragmentation: frequently adding/removing components scatters entities across many small archetype tables, destroying cache locality and degrading query performance to O(n).
Query over-matching: systems query for too broad a component set and waste cycles iterating entities they immediately skip, or query for too narrow a set and miss entities that should match.

Behaviour encapsulated in components: giving components methods and calling them directly reverts to an EC (Entity-Component) framework, losing the cache locality and data-oriented benefits of true ECS systems.

Synchronous structural changes during dispatch: adding or removing components mid-frame invalidates iterators and causes entities to appear in or disappear from systems unexpectedly within the same pass.
Premature data-oriented conversion: redesigning components into SoA layouts before profiling confirms cache pressure, adding complexity for a problem that does not exist at the current entity count.
design_principles: Composition over inheritance: capabilities are owned and delegated to, not inherited.
Single responsibility: one component per domain, and the container coordinates instead of implementing.
Open/closed: new behaviour arrives as a new component (and, in the systems form, a new system) without editing existing entities or components.
Separation of concerns: input, physics, rendering and audio code never see each other.
Dependency inversion: the container depends on component abstractions, never on concrete component types.
Information hiding: shared state is exposed deliberately, one owner per field, instead of being reachable by every component by convention.
Law of Least Knowledge: components collaborate through the container or the shared state, not through a web of sibling references.
best_practices: Define a minimal component contract (activate/update/deactivate, or a single update hook) and keep a component's own state inside the component.
Keep pan-domain state small and explicit; anything a component may touch on the container is a documented part of the container's surface.
Attach components in one place - a prefab, factory or assembler - never with scattered AddComponent-style calls at call sites.
Make required components explicit: validate the bundle at assembly time, or expose queries that only return entities carrying every component the system needs.
Never add or remove components while a dispatch pass is iterating; collect structural changes and apply them at a defined point (deferred commands, sync point, end of frame).
Choose the dispatch model deliberately - per-entity forwarding when order does not matter, per-component-type systems when it does - and write the order down.
Give every shared field one writer; when two components need to change it, route the change through the owner or through an explicit event.
Move to data-oriented storage (per-type pools, queries, archetypes) only after profiling shows component layout is the bottleneck, and then keep components plain data.
Store components as plain data (SoA layout) rather than encapsulating them in classes with methods; behaviour lives in systems, not components.
Prefer archetype-based queries (table/column storage) for cache-friendly iteration over large entity sets; use sparse-set storage when add/remove performance matters more.
Design components with single responsibility and data locality in mind: group fields accessed together in the same component to benefit from spatial locality.
Use tags (zero-size components) for marker types rather than boolean fields or enum discriminators to keep storage lean and queries fast.
Batch structural changes (add/remove component, create/destroy entity) and apply them at sync points to avoid archetype fragmentation and iterator invalidation.
When two systems need the same field, declare one as the authoritative writer and have the other read or subscribe via an event or signal.
sources: Nystrom (2014), Game Programming Patterns, 'Decoupling Patterns: Component' - the originating catalogue entry: intent ('allow a single entity to span multiple domains without coupling the domains to each other'), motivation, the three component-communication strategies and their consequences. https://gameprogrammingpatterns.com/component.html

Java Design Patterns catalogue, 'Component Pattern in Java' (also known as Entity-Component-System, Component-Entity-System, Component-Based Architecture) - the GameObject/component-classes rendering of the same structure. https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/component/

Apple, GameplayKit Programming Guide: Entities and Components - a first-party realization (GKEntity as a container for components, GKComponent, GKComponentSystem for per-component-type updates). https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/General/Conceptual/GameplayKit_Guide/EntityComponent.html

Unity, Manual: The GameObject class - 'a container for functional components which determine how the GameObject looks and what it does', with AddComponent/GetComponent. https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/class-GameObject.html
Baeldung, The Cake Pattern - Scala's component-trait/self-type elaboration of the same composition idea. https://www.baeldung.com/scala/cake-pattern
Sander Mertens, Flecs - a C99 entity component system whose vocabulary (world, entity, component, query, system) is the data-oriented elaboration. https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/

Wikipedia, 'Entity component system' - software architectural pattern definition, comparison with OOP, and overview of ECS vs Entity-Component frameworks. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity_component_system

Sander Mertens, 'Entity Component System FAQ' - comprehensive community FAQ covering ECS vs OOP, storage implementations (archetype, sparse-set, bitset), data-oriented design, cache locality, multithreading, and a curated list of ECS frameworks and real-world users. https://github.com/SanderMertens/ecs-faq

Mertens et al., 'The Essence of Entity Component System' (arXiv, 2026) - formal analysis of ECS semantics, archetype-based storage, query mechanisms, and performance characteristics. https://arxiv.org/html/2606.14919v1

Unity, 'Data-Oriented Design' - Unity's official DoD resources explaining SoA vs AoS layout, archetype storage, cache locality, and how DOTS leverages these principles. https://learn.unity.com/tutorial/part-1-understand-data-oriented-design

Unreal Engine, 'Mass Entity overview' - Epic's data-oriented ECS for Unreal Engine 5 covering archetype-based entity storage, fragment composition, and parallel processing. https://docs.unrealengine.com/5.0/en-US/overview-of-mass-entity-in-unreal-engine/

Fabian, 'Data Oriented Design' (online book) - the definitive text on DoD principles: cache lines, locality of reference, SIMD vectorization, SoA/AoS trade-offs, and why they matter for ECS. https://www.dataorienteddesign.com/dodbook/

Voelter, 'ECS vs OOP' - practical comparison of entity-component-system with object-oriented programming, covering composition trade-offs, reusability, and multithreading benefits. https://www.voelter.de/articles/ecs-vs-oop/

Our Machinery, 'ECS and Rendering' - practical discussion of integrating ECS with rendering pipelines, including transform hierarchies and data layout decisions. https://ourmachinery.com/post/ecs-and-rendering/

Sander Mertens, 'Why Vanilla ECS is not enough' - blog post on the limitations of plain ECS and the case for entity relationships, hierarchies, and built-in primitives. https://ajmmertens.medium.com/why-vanilla-ecs-is-not-enough-d7ed4e3bebe5

Bevy Engine, 'ECS' quick-start - official docs: entities as IDs, components as plain Rust structs in a World, systems as functions whose parameters drive parallel scheduling. https://bevy.org/learn/quick-start/getting-started/ecs/

Unity, 'Entities package' (com.unity.entities) official documentation - the DOTS data-oriented ECS realization with archetype storage, used for large entity populations. https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.entities@latest/
skypjack, 'EnTT' - header-only C++20 ECS with dense storage; README documents real adopters including Mojang's Minecraft and Esri ArcGIS SDKs. https://github.com/skypjack/entt

Moonside Games, 'Archetypal ECS Considered Harmful?' - critique showing archetype ECS's performance claims hold only in narrow patterns, with a measured regression case from dynamic composition. https://moonside.games/posts/archetypal-ecs-considered-harmful/

Voxagon Blog, 'Thoughts on ECS' - critique of the locality guarantee: multi-component systems pay multiple cache misses, and structural changes cost data movement and invalidation. https://blog.voxagon.se/2025-03-28/thoughts-on-ecs.html
